# Canonical list of paths an agent must NOT change without human review.
#
# Read by scripts/classify-pr-risk.sh, which the `risk-tier` CI job runs on every
# PR. A PR touching any of these is tier=high: it is never auto-merged, and the
# job annotates the PR with exactly which rule matched.
#
# .github/CODEOWNERS mirrors this list to auto-request review. Keep the two in
# step — CODEOWNERS cannot be generated from this file because required
# code-owner review needs GitHub Pro on a private repo (see
# scripts/enable-branch-protection.sh).
#
# Syntax: one path per line. A trailing /** matches the whole subtree.
# Blank lines and # comments ignored.
#
# The test for inclusion is: "if an agent got this wrong, would it breach auth,
# corrupt data, or break every future deploy?" Feature code fails that test and
# is deliberately absent — the point is autonomy everywhere else.

# ── Auth and access control ────────────────────────────────────────────
# hooks.server.ts owns the request gate; auth.ts owns PUBLIC_PATHS. A wrong
# edit here is how /admin ends up publicly readable.
src/hooks.server.ts
src/lib/auth.ts
src/lib/server/**
# The MCP bridge is the OTHER auth surface: /api/mcp* deliberately bypasses the
# Auth.js gate as service-to-service traffic, so bridge-token verification in
# here is the only thing standing between an anonymous POST and the whole tool
# catalogue (or tool execution). Added 2026-07-25 after a change to exactly this
# file would otherwise have classified low and auto-merged.
src/lib/mcp/**

# PUBLIC_PATHS is PREFIX-matched, so whole trees (/api/agent, /api/scraper,
# /projects, /decks, /jkai/shared, /dav) are ALREADY past the Auth.js gate. For
# those the only thing between an anonymous request and the data is a small
# self-gating helper — and hooks.server.ts DELEGATES to these, so protecting the
# hook without them protects nothing. Each is 1-2 commits in 2,294, and between
# them they are the entire control for the private DfE/Keystone work, private
# decks, shared conversations and the WebDAV mount.
src/lib/agent/auth.ts
src/lib/webdav/auth.ts
src/lib/workflows/scraper/service-auth.ts
src/lib/workflows/webhook-secret.ts
src/lib/projects/guard.ts
src/lib/projects/visibility.ts
src/lib/projects/shares.ts
src/lib/decks/guard.ts
src/lib/decks/shares.ts
src/routes/jkai/shared/[token]/+page.server.ts
# Anonymous fetch relay that returns upstream bodies with `Access-Control-Allow-Origin: *`.
# Its domain allowlist is the only control, and it is precisely where a generated
# canvas build would be tempted to add a domain.
src/routes/api/jkai/cors/[...url]/+server.ts
# NOTE (deliberate gap): because PUBLIC_PATHS is prefix-matched, a NEW route file
# under an existing public prefix is anonymously reachable the moment it is
# created — no allowlist edit, so no rule here can catch it. That wants a CI
# assertion over route files, not a path rule.

# ── Secret handling and crypto envelopes ───────────────────────────────
# Each is the SOLE encryption boundary for a credential store whose ciphertext
# the agent can already reach through the datastore/DB tools. Weakening one — or
# adding a debug log of the plaintext — turns readable ciphertext into readable
# secrets: Gmail refresh tokens, integration OAuth credentials, and the scraper
# vault's logins for third-party sites. One commit each; feature work for those
# areas lives in their runners and route handlers, never here.
src/lib/integrations/crypto.ts
src/lib/workflows/gmail/crypto.ts
src/lib/workflows/scraper/crypto.ts
# The same HMAC bridge-token mechanism protected above as src/lib/mcp/**, on a
# second route pair nobody had noticed: signs/verifies JKAI_BRIDGE_SECRET for the
# builder sidecar.
src/lib/jkai/tool-bridge.ts

# ── Data model ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# deploy runs `drizzle-kit push --force` against production, so a bad schema
# edit is applied to the live database automatically.
src/lib/db/schema.ts
drizzle.config.ts

# ── Build, deploy and CI ───────────────────────────────────────────────
# These decide what ships and how. An agent editing its own deploy path or its
# own gate can disable the checks that constrain it.
scripts/**
.github/**
.githooks/**
package.json
package-lock.json
vite.config.ts
svelte.config.js

# ── Agent self-modification: code that reaches production ──────────────
# `node_builder_commit_and_deploy` pushes straight to origin/master and runs
# scripts/deploy.sh — it never opens a PR, so the risk-tier job NEVER SEES IT.
# NODE_BUILDER_PATH_ALLOWLIST is the only bound on what it may write, so adding
# 'src/' or '.github/' to it converts the agent's own codegen into an
# arbitrary-file, direct-to-production channel that routes around this entire
# mechanism — including protected-paths.txt itself. This is the one escalation
# that defeats the gate rather than merely widening tool reach.
src/lib/workflows/site-tools/tools/node-builder-shared.ts
src/lib/workflows/site-tools/tools/node-builder.ts
# The allowlist of repos an autonomous build may clone, branch and push to, and
# the second independent repo pin used by the Forge.
src/lib/jkai/git-targets.ts
src/lib/jkai/forge.ts
# The only `git push` and the only PR-open path in the entire app, plus the
# container flags for the build sandbox. Higher churn than the rest of this
# section, but it is the chokepoint for everything an agent ships.
src/lib/jkai/sandbox.ts

# ── Agent safety rails ─────────────────────────────────────────────────
# The denylist and confirmation gate are what stop tool-calls doing damage.
# Self-modification of these must always be a human decision.
src/lib/workflows/nodes/site-tool-denylist.ts
src/lib/workflows/chat/confirmation-gate.ts
# site-tool.ts is the ONLY runtime enforcement of that denylist and of the
# destructive/upstream-approval rule. Protecting the denylist DATA but not its
# enforcement was the gap — the data file is inert without this.
src/lib/workflows/nodes/site-tool.ts
# schedule_tool_at refuses destructive tools; deferred calls fire with no LLM
# round, no confirmation UI and no user present, and no test covers this guard.
src/lib/workflows/site-tools/tools/scheduled.ts
# The only in-process sandbox boundary for LLM/user-authored workflow
# expressions (`new Function`, same process as the server). Both its commits
# were security hardening.
src/lib/workflows/nodes/safe-eval.ts
# Outbound-network boundary for the /jkai chat agent, holding SSRF enforcement
# that src/lib/server/ssrf-guard.ts does not.
src/lib/workflows/site-tools/tools/apis.ts
# TESTS AS INVARIANTS. site-tools/tools/** is 96 commits in six months — it IS
# ordinary feature work and protecting it would end the autonomy. But that is
# where every `destructive: true` literal lives. These two tests pin the flags
# and the llm-agent exclusion, so dropping a flag fails CI instead of
# auto-merging. Protecting the assertions costs a fraction of protecting the
# subtree, and without them one PR could delete a flag AND its assertion.
src/lib/workflows/site-tools/toolchain-fixes.test.ts
tests/lib/workflows/nodes/llm-agent-site-tools.test.ts
